procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Gwalior in MCRC No.20941 of 2017, dated 20.11.2017, and another unspecified order.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The first respondent (accused) challenged the Magistrate's order (rejecting his application) before the High Court. A Division Bench of the High Court held that when a charge sheet was filed in a language unknown to the accused, he was entitled to a translation of the charge sheet in a language he understands.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) appealed the High Court's orders to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court set aside the impugned orders of the High Court and directed the Trial Court to expeditiously proceed with the trial.

directions: The impugned orders are set aside.
There will be no order as to costs.
The Trial Court shall expeditiously proceed with the trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the orders of the Magistrate and Sessions Court and directing the supply of a Hindi translation of the charge sheet filed in English, on the grounds that Hindi was the only language of the Criminal Courts in Madhya Pradesh.

facts: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) filed charge sheets in English in cases related to the Vyapam Scam in Madhya Pradesh.
The accused-respondents filed applications requesting a Hindi translation of the charge sheet, claiming they could not understand English.

The Magistrate and the Sessions Court rejected these applications, noting that the accused were educated, had knowledge of English (one had even signed his legal documents in English), and were represented by lawyers who knew English.

The High Court overturned these decisions, ruling that since Hindi is the designated language of the Criminal Courts in Madhya Pradesh, the accused were entitled to a translation of the charge sheet into the language of the court.
law: The Supreme Court clarified the scope of Section 272 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). It held that this section only determines the language to be used by the *Court* in its proceedings.

Section 272 does not grant power to the State Government to decide the language that investigating agencies (like the police or CBI) must use for their investigation records, including the charge sheet filed under Section 173 CrPC.
The Court noted that there is no provision in the CrPC that makes it mandatory for a charge sheet to be filed in the language of the court.
A charge sheet filed in a language other than the court's language is not illegal and cannot be a ground for default bail.

An accused is entitled to a translation, but this right is conditional. The accused must satisfy the court that they are genuinely unable to understand the language of the charge sheet and that its non-supply would lead to a failure of justice.
application: The Supreme Court applied the law to the specific facts of the case and found that the High Court's reasoning was flawed.
It agreed with the initial findings of the Magistrate that the accused were educated individuals with knowledge of English.

The Court determined that, in this specific case, the non-supply of a Hindi translation would not cause a "failure of justice" because the accused were capable of understanding the English charge sheet and were represented by competent counsel.
Therefore, the accused had not met the condition of proving they were unable to understand the language of the charge sheet.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision. It held that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the lower courts' orders because the language of the court (Hindi) does not mandate that the charge sheet must also be in that language. Since the accused could not prove they were unable to understand English, they were not entitled to a translation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the orders of the Magistrate and Sessions Court and directing the supply of a Hindi translation of the charge sheet filed in English, on the grounds that Hindi was the only language of the Criminal Courts in Madhya Pradesh.
appellant_arguments: The supply of a translated charge sheet is not an absolute right and should only be provided if the accused can satisfy the court that they are unable to understand the language of the original charge sheet.
In the specific facts of this case, the accused were educated individuals with knowledge of English; one was a science graduate and the other was taking an exam that required English proficiency.
The advocates for the accused were also conversant with the English language.
Given these facts, the non-supply of a Hindi translation of the charge sheet and other documents would not cause a failure of justice.
respondent_arguments: Under Section 272 of the CrPC, the State Government of Madhya Pradesh has declared Hindi as the only language of the Criminal Courts.
Consequently, charge sheets filed under Section 173 of the CrPC ought to be in Hindi, the designated language of the court.

If an accused is not provided with a charge sheet in a language they understand, they cannot properly defend themselves, as they would be unable to comprehend the police statements and other evidence collected during the investigation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When deciding if a procedural irregularity has caused a failure of justice, the court must consider whether the objection was raised at the earliest available opportunity.
obiter: Under Section 354, it is provided that judgment in every trial of a Criminal Court must be written in the language of the Court.
When documents are put for the purpose of formal proof, it shall be in the discretion of the Court to interpret as much thereof as appears necessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: If a document, such as a charge sheet, is provided in a language other than the designated language of the court, the proceedings are not automatically vitiated. Such a procedural omission only invalidates the proceedings if it is established that the omission has resulted in a failure of justice. On the facts of this case, the non-supply of a Hindi translation of the English charge sheet and other documents to the accused would not occasion a failure of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The 'failure of justice' test, as incorporated in Section 465 of the CrPC, is applied to any error, omission, or irregularity in proceedings. Proceedings will not be vitiated unless the omission has in fact resulted in a failure of justice.
When determining if a failure of justice has occurred, the court must consider whether the objection was raised at the earliest available opportunity.
The burden is on the accused to satisfy the court that they are unable to understand the language in which the charge sheet is submitted to justify the provision of a translation.
policy_considerations: The judicial policy is that proceedings should not be invalidated due to a procedural irregularity, such as using a language other than that of the court, unless it is proven that this irregularity has caused an actual failure of justice.
